title: Llevar vs Traer: Take or Bring in Spanish?
seo_title: Llevar vs Traer: Take or Bring in Spanish?
meta_description: Llevar vs traer: Spanish decides between take and bring by where the speaker is. Clear rules, examples, other meanings of llevar, mistakes and a quick quiz.
excerpt: Spanish chooses between “take” and “bring” by where you are. Here’s the simple rule.

body_html:
Llevar vs traer trips up learners because English is relaxed about “take” and “bring”, while Spanish is strict. The rule depends on location: traer means to bring something here, toward the speaker, and llevar means to take something there, away from the speaker. Once you picture an arrow pointing toward you or away from you, the choice becomes almost automatic.

Quick answer
  • Traer = bring (toward where the speaker is): ¿Me traes agua?
  • Llevar = take, carry (away from the speaker): Llevo el vino a la fiesta.
  • English “I’ll bring the wine to your party” is Llevaré el vino in Spanish, because you are going there.
  • Llevar also means to wear, to spend time and more.
{{toc}}

Llevar vs traer: the core rule

TraerLlevar
DirectionToward the speaker (here)Away from the speaker (there)
Englishto bringto take, to carry
ExampleTrae tu guitarra a mi casa. Bring your guitar to my house.Lleva tu guitarra a casa de Ana. Take your guitar to Ana’s house.

Think of it as an arrow. If the object moves to where you are (or where you will be, if you are the host), use traer. If it moves somewhere else, use llevar.

Where English and Spanish disagree

English often says “bring” when Spanish insists on llevar:

  • “I’ll bring a cake to your party.” → Llevaré una tarta a tu fiesta. (You are going there.)
  • “Can you bring the kids to school?” → ¿Puedes llevar a los niños al colegio? (School is not where the speaker is.)
  • “Bring me a coffee, please.” → Tráeme un café, por favor. (Toward the speaker: traer.)

When the host speaks, the party location counts as “here”: ¿Qué vas a traer a mi fiesta? (What are you going to bring to my party?). The guest answers from their own position: Voy a llevar una ensalada. Both are correct.

{{image:2}}

Other meanings of llevar

Llevar is a busy verb. The RAE dictionary lists dozens of uses; these are the ones you will hear most:

  • To wear: Lleva lentes. She wears glasses.
  • To spend time: Llevo dos años en Madrid. I’ve been in Madrid for two years.
  • Still doing (+ gerund): Llevo una hora esperando. I’ve been waiting for an hour.
  • To contain: ¿Qué lleva esta salsa? What’s in this sauce?
  • To get along: Me llevo muy bien con mi hermana. I get on very well with my sister.
  • To take away (food): Un café para llevar. A coffee to go.

Conjugation note

Llevar is regular. Traer is irregular: traigo, traes, trae… in the present, and traje, trajiste, trajo, trajeron in the past. Commands: trae / tráeme, lleva / llévate.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Real conversations

Planning a dinner

  • Host: Para la cena del sábado, ¿puedes traer el postre? (For Saturday’s dinner, can you bring dessert?)
  • Guest: Claro, llevo una tarta de chocolate. ¿Llevo también vino? (Sure, I’ll bring a chocolate cake. Shall I bring wine too?)
  • Host: No hace falta, ya tengo. Solo tráete a ti mismo. (No need, I already have some. Just bring yourself.)

Leaving the house

  • A: Va a llover. Llévate el paraguas. (It’s going to rain. Take the umbrella.)
  • B: Está bien. ¿Te traigo algo del súper? (Okay. Shall I bring you anything from the supermarket?)

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Voy a traer vino a tu fiesta.Voy a llevar vino a tu fiesta.You’re going there
Llévame un vaso de agua. (meaning “bring me”)Tráeme un vaso de agua.Toward the speaker
Traje a mi hijo al colegio. (said at home)Llevé a mi hijo al colegio.School isn’t “here”
Un café para traerUn café para llevarFixed expression

A note on variation: in casual speech, especially on the phone, some speakers in parts of Latin America use traer more loosely, closer to English. Following the speaker-location rule is always correct.

{{image:3}}

Llevar vs traer at a restaurant

Restaurants give you daily practice. Ask the waiter to bring things to your table with traer: ¿Nos trae la carta, por favor? (Could you bring us the menu, please?), ¿Me trae otra servilleta? (Could you bring me another napkin?). When you want leftovers boxed up, use llevar: ¿Me lo da para llevar? (Could you pack it to go?). In Spain you’ll also hear ¿Me lo pone para llevar?

The same logic: ir and venir

Llevar and traer follow exactly the same logic as {{link:ir-vs-venir|ir vs venir}}: venir and traer point toward the speaker; ir and llevar point away. Learn them as a set and both become easier. For more pairs like this, see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}, or the related {{link:pedir-vs-preguntar|pedir vs preguntar}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

To choose between llevar vs traer, picture yourself and draw an arrow. Toward you: traer. Away from you: llevar. Add the extra meanings of llevar (wearing, spending time, getting along) and you have one of Spanish’s most useful verbs under control.

faq.q: What is the difference between llevar and traer?
faq.a: Traer means to bring something toward where the speaker is. Llevar means to take or carry something away from the speaker to another place.

faq.q: Do I use llevar or traer when bringing food to a party?
faq.a: Llevar, because you are going to the party: Voy a llevar una ensalada. The host, speaking from the party location, would say ¿Qué vas a traer?
Para llevar means “to go” or “takeaway”, as in un café para llevar.

questions.q: You are at home. ¿Me ___ un vaso de agua, por favor?
questions.explain: The water comes toward you: traer.

questions.q: You are going to a friend’s party. Voy a ___ una tarta.
questions.explain: You are taking it there: llevar.

questions.q: Un café para ___, por favor. (to go)
questions.explain: Para llevar is the fixed expression for takeaway.

questions.q: ___ tres años viviendo aquí. (I’ve been living here for three years.)
The host says: ¿Qué vas a ___ a mi cumpleaños?
questions.explain: The host speaks from the party location, so the gift comes “here”: traer.
